```{r setup, include = FALSE}
has_sf <- requireNamespace("sf", quietly = TRUE)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = has_sf,
                      fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4.6, dpi = 80)
library(rPSTool)
```

## 1. What rPSTool does

rPSTool is an R interface to the C++ analysis engine of the *Place Syntax Tool*
(PST). The package compiles a pinned copy of the engine (PST v3.3.2) and calls
it directly, so installing it needs neither QGIS nor a separate PST
installation. rPSTool does not reimplement the algorithms: you build a graph from
your lines, the engine analyses it, and R receives the engine's results.
This vignette walks through one small workflow on the example data that ships
with the package: inspect the data, build an axial graph, run Network
Integration, attach the results to the map and draw it.

The example data are `sf` objects, so the package **sf** is needed to run the
code below. It is an optional dependency of rPSTool; if it is not installed the
code chunks in this vignette are skipped.

```{r no-sf, echo = FALSE, eval = !has_sf, results = "asis"}
cat("**The sf package is not installed, so the code chunks in this vignette",
    "were not run.**\n")
```

## 2. Load the example data

`load_example_data()` takes no arguments and returns a list of three `sf`
objects for the Barnsbury area of London.

```{r load}
ex <- load_example_data()
names(ex)
vapply(ex, nrow, integer(1))
sf::st_crs(ex$axial)$epsg
```

## 3. Inspect the data

The three components are the **axial map** (one line per axial line), the
**unlinks** (points where two axial lines cross without being connected) and
the **gate observations** (movement counts and street attributes at gates).

```{r inspect}
names(ex$axial)
names(ex$unlinks)
names(ex$gates)
head(sf::st_drop_geometry(ex$axial), 3)
```

All three are in British National Grid (EPSG:27700, metres). Some points to
keep in mind.

* The four `source_*` columns of `ex$axial` (connectivity, control,
  integration, local integration) are **historical values supplied with the
  data**, kept unchanged. They are not rPSTool or PST results, and no rPSTool
  function reads them.
* The axial map is from Hillier and Iida (2005). The pedestrian and vehicle
  movement observations in `ex$gates` were originally used in Penn, Hillier,
  Banister and Xu (1998). The geometry was **georeferenced to British National
  Grid and spatially transformed** by Kimon Krenz, so the coordinates are *not*
  the original coordinates of the source data.
* `axial_id` is the original axial-line identifier. In general identifiers are
  unique but are not row numbers; `?hillier_iida` describes all columns.

## 4. Build an axial graph

`axial_graph()` hands the lines to the engine, which finds where they cross
and keeps the resulting network in memory. Two inputs matter here. The
**axial lines** define the network: two axial lines are connected where they
cross. The **unlinks** list crossings that are *not* connections (for example
where one street passes over another), and the engine removes them. Passing
them gives the intended network.

```{r graph}
g <- axial_graph(ex$axial, unlinks = ex$unlinks)
g
```

Things worth knowing about the graph:

* It lives in native memory managed by the engine; the R object holds a
  pointer to it, plus the counts printed above. It is released when R
  garbage-collects the object, and copying the R object shares the same
  native graph.
* It cannot be saved with `saveRDS()` or sent to another R process; rebuild it
  from the data instead.
* Build it once and reuse it. Every analysis below takes `g` and costs only
  the analysis itself.
* rPSTool does no snapping, splitting or reprojection. Each `sf` feature must be a
  straight line of exactly two vertices, as in this dataset.

## 5. Run Network Integration

`network_integration()` is the axial-map analysis. For every line it relates
the topological distances (number of line changes, "steps") to all reached
lines to the number of lines reached. Here it is run twice: unrestricted
(every line reaches every other line), and with a radius limited to three
steps. `analysis_radius()` describes the limits; `steps = 3` is the only one
set.

```{r integration}
whole  <- network_integration(g)
local3 <- network_integration(g, radius = analysis_radius(steps = 3))
head(whole)
```

The result has one row per input line and the columns `line_id`, `integration`,
`node_count` (the number of lines reached, including the line itself) and
`total_depth` (the sum of the steps to the reached lines). The engine returns
`-1` where fewer than two lines are reached, and it may return `NaN` or `Inf`
for very small neighbourhoods; rPSTool passes these through unchanged.

```{r summary}
rbind(unrestricted = summary(whole$integration),
      steps_3      = summary(local3$integration))
range(whole$node_count)
range(local3$node_count)
```

The step-limited run reaches fewer lines from each line, which is why its
`node_count` is smaller.

## 6. Join the results to the geometry

The results are an ordinary data frame without geometry. Rows are in the same
order as the lines you gave to `axial_graph()`, and `line_id` is the one-based
row index of that input. So the *i*th result row belongs to the *i*th row of
`ex$axial`, whatever its `axial_id`:

```{r join}
stopifnot(identical(whole$line_id, seq_len(nrow(ex$axial))))
map <- ex$axial
map$integration <- whole$integration
map$integration_3 <- local3$integration
```

Join by position (or by `line_id`), not by `axial_id`: the two coincide in this
dataset only because its identifiers happen to run from 1 to the number of
lines. Do not rely on that for other data.

## 7. Draw the map

`colour_map()` turns numbers into colours from an rPSTool palette. It does not
classify; with the default continuous mapping the range of the values is
spread linearly over the palette (or over `limits`, if you give them). The
plot background is your choice. Coral Day is designed for light backgrounds
and Coral Night for dark ones (`colour_palettes()$background` lists the
intended background of each palette).

```{r plot-day}
par(mar = c(0, 0, 1.5, 0))
plot(sf::st_geometry(map), col = colour_map(map$integration, "coral_day"),
     lwd = 1.5, main = "Integration, unrestricted (Coral Day)")
```

```{r plot-night}
par(mar = c(0, 0, 1.5, 0), bg = "black", fg = "white")
plot(sf::st_geometry(map), col = colour_map(map$integration_3, "coral_night"),
     lwd = 1.5, main = "Integration, 3 steps (Coral Night)", col.main = "white")
```

With ggplot2, `scale_colour_rpst_c()` applies the same continuous mapping:

```{r ggplot, eval = has_sf && requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(map) +
  geom_sf(aes(colour = integration_3), linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_colour_rpst_c("coral_day") +
  theme_void() +
  labs(colour = "Integration\n(3 steps)")
```

## 8. Interpreting the output

In PST's axial analysis a line with a high integration value is, by the
topological measure used, close to the other lines of the network (few changes
of direction are needed to reach them), and a low value means it is relatively
isolated. The values come from the engine's formula; rPSTool does not rescale
them. They are comparable between lines of the same run. The
step-limited run describes each line's local neighbourhood and the
unrestricted run its position in the whole network, so the two sets of values
answer different questions; compare values only within one run, and do not
assume that values from different radii or different graphs share a scale.

The example data come with a historical integration value for each line
(`source_integration`). You can compare it with the rPSTool result as a purely
descriptive check on the data you have just joined; this is a comparison, not
a validation of either set of numbers.

```{r compare}
cor(whole$integration, map$source_integration)
cor(whole$integration, map$source_integration, method = "spearman")
max(abs(whole$integration - map$source_integration))
```

In this run the unrestricted result and the supplied column agree closely: both
correlations are 1 to the printed precision, and the largest absolute difference
is about 6e-06. Whether the supplied values were produced the same way is not
documented in the package, and this agreement should not be read as a statement
about published results. The supplied `source_local_integration` is a different
quantity and is not compared here.

The unlinks matter. Building the graph without them leaves two more crossings
in the graph (each one a connection between two lines), which changes the
network the engine analyses:

```{r unlinks-effect}
c(with_unlinks = g$n_crossings,
  without_unlinks = axial_graph(ex$axial)$n_crossings)
```

## 9. Where next

* `?rPSTool` gives an overview of the package and links to its function groups.
* `vignette("pst-capabilities", package = "rPSTool")` compares rPSTool with the
  engine and the PST plugin for QGIS and shows the other analyses (reach,
  betweenness, angular analyses, attraction analyses, segment maps).
* The function reference lists every function; start with `?axial_graph`,
  `?network_integration`, `?analysis_radius`, `?colour_map` and
  `?hillier_iida`.
